candidate_population.title: Reshaping the African Internet: From scattered islands to a connected continent

verified_extraction.claim_path: The paper starts from poor African traffic locality and low peering participation, shows that a distance-minimizing IXP topology is not practically realizable, parameterizes political, geographic, fiber and investment constraints, and simulates a four-step distributed-IXP build-out to estimate best-case path and latency changes.
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Evidence combines a survey sent to all 37 identified African IXP operators with 22 responses, public IXP/member/fiber/cable/investment/security datasets, a March 2016 CAIDA topology of 53,537 ASes and 215,628 links, traceroute-derived AS-link RTT distributions, an analysis subgraph of 1,389 ASes and 10,756 links, and 1,725 propagated prefixes. IXP membership data were validated by responding operators where possible.
verified_extraction.quantitative_behavior: In the simulation, continental intra-African paths rise from 40% initially to 51.2%, 69.5%, and 94% after steps 1-3; the mode of intra-African AS-path length falls from 4 to 2; the modeled median of mean intra-African RTT falls from 144.1 ms initially to 58.92 ms after step 1 and 61.1 ms after step 3. These are counterfactual topology and estimated-RTT results, not observed production traffic outcomes.
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Feasible links and benefits depend on existing submarine and terrestrial fiber, country security classification, investment, geography, IXP membership, sub-regional cooperation, ISP incentives and content-provider presence. A five-year security threshold was tested against one-, three- and ten-year windows, but transfer to other regions requires new domain-specific data and constraints.
verified_extraction.causal_calibration: The design compares simulated counterfactual topologies rather than identifying a causal effect from a realized deployment. Customer-cone rules approximate willingness to peer; the authors explicitly expect fewer real peering links because pricing, competition and bilateral strategy are omitted.
limitations: No interdomain traffic-volume data are included, so the analysis cannot say how much traffic would actually shift onto shorter paths.
Each AS is modeled as a single router; intradomain topology and routing are excluded.
RTTs on AS links are inferred from traceroute samples and are acknowledged as approximations rather than precise values.
Political and socioeconomic factors are incomplete and time-varying; the analysis requires periodic refresh.
Public IXP membership data are not uniformly operator-validated.
Peering economics are reduced to a customer-cone constraint; real adoption and link creation can be materially lower.
The step-3 spanning tree is not redundant and would require added links, a ring/full mesh and backup hubs for outage robustness.
Cost estimates are back-of-the-envelope and economic sustainability is left for future work.
anti_patterns: Do not equate IXP presence or listed membership with an active peering relationship or carried traffic.
Do not present modeled best-case RTT and path improvements as observed deployment effects.
Do not optimize route length without political, commercial, fiber and repair feasibility constraints.
Do not treat multiple logical links or a spanning tree as independent physical redundancy.
Do not infer traffic volume, usable local capacity or campus-level service from AS-path counts.
Do not transfer the Africa-specific topology solution to another region without rebuilding its constraints and datasets.

candidate_population.title: A worldwide study on the geographic locality of Internet routes
candidate_population.candidate_study_type: large-scale active measurement and route-geolocation analysis

verified_extraction.study_type: RIPE Atlas active-measurement, IP geolocation and country-level route-locality analysis
verified_extraction.claim_path: The study defines route locality at region and country scales, geolocates hops in roughly 1.5 million RIPE Atlas traceroutes, and compares locality under address-space and population weighting to show that geographic endpoint proximity does not guarantee geographically local routing.
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Traceroute paths from RIPE Atlas are evaluated by endpoints and intermediate hops; country results are separately weighted by routed address space and population. Missing or uncertain hop geolocations are treated conservatively, and the reported population/address-space summaries are not traffic-volume shares.
verified_extraction.quantitative_behavior: Europe, North America and Oceania show substantially greater route locality than Africa, Asia, the Middle East and South America. The exact country ordering changes with endpoint availability, geolocation coverage and the selected address-space or population denominator.
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Locality varies across regions, countries, RIPE Atlas vantage coverage and weighting conventions. A path crossing a political boundary may be operationally short, while a geographically close endpoint pair may follow a distant interdomain route.
verified_extraction.causal_calibration: This is a descriptive measurement study; it establishes observed routing patterns within the sampled traces and does not identify the causal effect of adding a facility, IXP, cable or peering agreement.
limitations: RIPE Atlas probes and measurements are not a probability sample of users or traffic.
IP geolocation is incomplete and can be wrong, especially at router interfaces.
Ungeolocated hops and ambiguous borders can change locality classifications.
Traceroute exposes selected forwarding paths rather than all available paths or carried traffic.
Country, population and address-space weights answer different questions and cannot be substituted for local usable capacity.
anti_patterns: Do not infer route locality from endpoint distance.
Do not treat RIPE Atlas trace shares as traffic shares.
Do not present country locality as campus bandwidth or service availability.
Do not hide the effect of weighting and geolocation coverage.

candidate_population.title: Meta-Peering: Automating ISP Peering Decision Process
candidate_population.journal: IEEE Transactions on Network and Service Management

journal_impact_factor_gate.verification_note: Official IEEE title list reports the 2024 JCR value released in June 2025; this is safely above the binary 2.0 gate.

verified_extraction.study_type: public-data peering prediction framework with supervised learning and rule-based comparison
verified_extraction.claim_path: The paper operationalizes ISP peering decisions with geographic and relationship-aware predictors, trains and evaluates GEO-PP and RCA-PP using public CAIDA and PeeringDB data, and treats the output as decision support rather than proof that a bilateral peering agreement will materialize.
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: The principal evaluations use 1,324 U.S. ISP pairs with a strongly imbalanced 90:10 class split and a 1,528-pair balanced dataset near 47:53. CAIDA relationship labels and PeeringDB facilities are treated as public-data proxies, while population and distance features come from external geospatial datasets.
verified_extraction.quantitative_behavior: The machine-learning GEO-PP implementation reports balanced accuracy around 66% on the imbalanced U.S. setting and around 80% on the balanced setting; RCA-PP is lower and is computationally approximated. Predicted locations are a small candidate set, not an enumeration of every operational peering point.
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Results depend on class balance, geography, public-record completeness, model hyperparameters, topology and the set of candidate facilities. Commercial traffic, pricing, contractual terms and operator strategy are largely unavailable.
verified_extraction.causal_calibration: Prediction accuracy against inferred public labels is not causal evidence that co-location creates peering, traffic exchange or performance improvement.
limitations: CAIDA relationship inferences and PeeringDB entries can be incomplete or inaccurate.
Commercial policies, traffic ratios, price and contractual constraints are not fully observable.
Class imbalance materially changes accuracy interpretation.
The relationship-aware algorithm requires approximations to remain computationally practical.
Predicted agreements and locations require operator feedback and real-world validation.
anti_patterns: Do not equate co-location with willingness to peer.
Do not treat predicted peering as a signed agreement or carried traffic.
Do not report raw accuracy without the class balance.
Do not treat public facility records as complete operational ground truth.

candidate_population.title: GAFA's information infrastructure distribution: Interconnection dynamics in the global North versus global South

verified_extraction.study_type: global PeeringDB infrastructure inventory with descriptive statistics and probit models
verified_extraction.claim_path: The study maps publicly listed interconnection points and ports for Google, Amazon, Facebook and Apple, compares the global North and South, and tests whether country wealth predicts public presence while explicitly bounding the analysis to visible interconnection.
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: PeeringDB observations were captured on 17 March 2020, yielding 1,357 company-location observations across IXPs and private facilities. Presence, port count and listed speed describe public records, not the companies’ full private backbone, caches, traffic or services.
verified_extraction.quantitative_behavior: About 77.9% of observed points lie in the global North; approximately 38% of North countries and 16% of South countries have a listed GAFA public point. Apple is about 92% North, Amazon 82.5%, Facebook 73% and Google 72%; per-capita GNI is the strongest modeled predictor.
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Company patterns differ, with Google and Facebook relatively broader in the South and port-speed patterns unlike Apple and Amazon. Results are a 2020 public-data snapshot shaped by voluntary updates and company architecture.
verified_extraction.causal_calibration: The probit associations do not show that wealth causes deployment; market size, regulation, demand, private facilities, caches and internal design remain intertwined.
limitations: PeeringDB is voluntary and update incentives vary.
Private interconnection, CDN deployments and Google Global Cache can be invisible.
A listed point need not expose every company service.
Port speed is a ceiling/proxy, not observed carried traffic.
The study cannot observe internal topology or all company-owned infrastructure.
anti_patterns: Do not call public listings a complete hyperscaler footprint.
Do not convert port speed to realized traffic or local capacity.
Do not infer service reach from one listed facility.
Do not interpret North-South associations as causal deployment effects.

candidate_population.title: Nautilus: A Framework for Cross-Layer Cartography of Submarine Cables and IP Links
candidate_population.journal: Proceedings of the ACM on Measurement and Analysis of Computing Systems

verified_extraction.study_type: cross-layer Internet measurement framework with multi-dataset inference and failure/operator-map validation
verified_extraction.claim_path: Nautilus combines traceroutes, IP geolocation, landing-point proximity, cable metadata and ownership evidence to infer candidate submarine cables for logical IP links and attach confidence rather than asserting a one-to-one observed physical route.
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: The framework first classifies links as submarine, terrestrial or uncertain, then ranks cable candidates. Reported coverage and validation denominators refer to the study datasets and resolvable links, not all Internet traffic or all active cable segments.
verified_extraction.quantitative_behavior: The framework maps 81% of identified submarine or unconfirmed links; mapped links average 2.04 candidate cables, with 76% having at most two and 93% at most five. Validation recovered 31 of 34 Tata and 52 of 58 Vodafone operator-map associations, but these are selected validation sets.
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Confidence varies with endpoint geolocation quality, landing-point density, owner information, MPLS visibility and the availability of a terrestrial alternative. Roughly 55% of classified links remain potential submarine links because a terrestrial route cannot be excluded.
verified_extraction.causal_calibration: Failure co-movement and operator maps validate selected associations but do not turn every mapping into physical ground truth or prove independent-route resilience.
limitations: City-level IP geolocation is only roughly 50-60% accurate in the cited evidence.
MPLS and hidden hops obscure the logical-to-physical mapping.
Cable and ownership datasets are incomplete and time-varying.
Multiple cables often remain plausible for one IP link.
Proximity to a landing point and ownership matching are inference features, not direct observation.
anti_patterns: Do not map an IP hop deterministically to one cable without uncertainty.
Do not count candidate cables as independent paths.
Do not interpret mapping coverage as traffic coverage.
Do not treat a shared landing point or owner as route independence.

candidate_population.title: Climate change hotspots and implications for the global subsea telecommunications network

verified_extraction.study_type: global evidence synthesis and spatial climate-hazard hotspot assessment
verified_extraction.claim_path: The review integrates peer-reviewed global climate and ocean datasets with cable and landing-station exposure to identify where hazards may change over 20-30-year cable lives, emphasizing local and compound processes instead of one global risk multiplier.
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: The synthesis spans sea-level, storm, wave, current, sediment, ice, erosion and human-activity pathways. Hotspots are scenario- and dataset-conditioned exposure assessments, not observed failure probabilities for each cable.
verified_extraction.quantitative_behavior: The central result is pronounced spatial and temporal heterogeneity: not all regions change in the same direction, at the same rate or through the same hazard. Instantaneous events and sustained low-level abrasion/fatigue require separate treatment.
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Risk varies by local bathymetry, canyon/channel geometry, landing-station setting, tectonics, river sediment, climate scenario, human activity and design life. Narrow strategic corridors can prevent hazard avoidance.
verified_extraction.causal_calibration: Projected climate layers and case evidence identify plausible changing exposure; they do not causally estimate a cable-specific fault rate or outage duration.
limitations: Global source layers differ in resolution and uncertainty.
Climate feedbacks, natural processes and human responses interact nonlinearly.
Indirect climate effects on fishing and anchoring are not systematically recorded.
Local route surveys and asset details are needed for decisions.
Rare extremes are sparsely observed.
anti_patterns: Do not assign one climate-risk factor to every route.
Do not treat a hotspot as a predicted outage.
Do not ignore sustained low-intensity hazards.
Do not count geographically separate routes as independent without shared-hazard analysis.

candidate_population.title: The diversity, frequency and severity of natural hazard impacts on subsea telecommunications networks

verified_extraction.study_type: global industry fault-database analysis, forensic attribution and hazard synthesis
verified_extraction.claim_path: The study analyzes 5,817 industry-recorded cable faults from 1965-2019, isolates 1,473 potentially natural-hazard records, cross-references global datasets and case studies, and distinguishes frequent local stressors from rare correlated multi-cable disasters.
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: The database covers transmission-stopping or major-repair faults known to one industry source. Cause categories are assigned from repair evidence and inference; minor maintenance and unrecorded events are absent.
verified_extraction.quantitative_behavior: About 25% of database faults fall in natural or potentially natural categories. Natural hazards are less frequent than fishing and anchors but can synchronously damage long lengths and multiple systems; sustained currents and abrasion can accumulate without one extreme trigger.
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Severity depends on hazard type, depth, seabed, exposure duration, regional route diversity and landing concentration. Tectonic, meteorological and sediment processes can compound and cascade.
verified_extraction.causal_calibration: Historical attribution and spatial correspondence support mechanism diagnosis, not a complete actuarial failure model; several category labels can overlap or be misclassified.
limitations: Proprietary records are not a census of all global faults.
The classification scheme is coarse and partly subjective.
Some seismic labels may represent triggered landslides or turbidity currents.
Only service-stopping or major-repair events are included.
Global bathymetry smooths fine-scale terrain important to cables.
anti_patterns: Do not use 25% as a universal future fault probability.
Do not treat cause labels as error-free.
Do not infer resilience from total cable count.
Do not ignore correlated and delayed cascading damage.

candidate_population.title: Evaluating and refining undersea cable path planning algorithms: A comparative study

journal_impact_factor_gate.verification_note: PLOS confirms JIF availability but does not promote the number; the latest accessible JCR value was cross-checked as 2.8. The gate is used only as pass/fail.

verified_extraction.claim_path: The paper compares Fast Marching, Dijkstra-based and great-circle routes on weighted seafloor cost surfaces, showing that lower modeled cost depends on grid representation and runtime and remains an initial engineering route rather than a deployable cable plan.
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Experiments use gridded public bathymetric and hazard layers and compare accumulated weighted cost and computation time across route cases. The weights encode the study objective; they are not contracted construction prices or realized fault probabilities.
verified_extraction.quantitative_behavior: Fast Marching produces weighted costs about 2.1-28% below the Dijkstra implementation in the reported cases but takes roughly 1.5-3 times as long. Dijkstra results are sensitive to allowed grid directions and discretization.
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Route ranking changes with map resolution, hazard weights, endpoint geometry, diagonal movement rules and omitted engineering constraints. Great-circle distance is a geometric baseline, not a risk- or deployment-optimal route.
verified_extraction.causal_calibration: Algorithm comparison establishes behavior on modeled cost surfaces, not actual build cost, permitting, survey approval, lay feasibility or subsequent reliability.
limitations: Public ocean data can be too coarse for final routing.
The model omits detailed bending-radius, burial, permitting and private survey constraints.
Weighted costs depend on subjective or case-specific layer weights.
Runtime comparisons depend on implementation and grid resolution.
Human surveyors and engineering review remain necessary before deployment.
anti_patterns: Do not call the lowest modeled-cost path deployment-ready.
Do not convert weighted cost directly to dollars or fault probability.
Do not ignore grid-resolution and movement-rule sensitivity.
Do not infer physical redundancy from separately optimized lines without shared-risk analysis.

candidate_population.title: Global submarine cable network and digital divide
candidate_population.candidate_study_type: global network and spatial inequality analysis

verified_extraction.study_type: 1995-2023 multi-scale spatial and complex-network analysis of submarine cables and landing points
verified_extraction.claim_path: The paper combines TeleGeography and Infrapedia cable records, traces network evolution at country and landing-point levels, calculates centrality and community structure, and uses the resulting topology as one physical-infrastructure lens on the global digital divide.
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Nodes and links represent cataloged countries, landing points and cable connections, with capacity where reported. Centrality is averaged across four measures and years; it is a topology index rather than traffic, price, adoption or fault tolerance.
verified_extraction.quantitative_behavior: Cable quantity, capacity and landing-point distribution are highly concentrated; a small set of countries and landing points form the core, while large developing-country regions remain peripheral. Network communities and pairwise links show strong geographic clustering and proximity.
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Country-level centrality and landing-point centrality can disagree: many European landings are peripheral individually despite strong national/regional infrastructure, while Mumbai, Fujairah, Jeddah, Hong Kong and Singapore serve major gateway roles.
verified_extraction.causal_calibration: The topology documents infrastructure distribution and evolution but cannot establish that a cable causes digital inclusion, economic empowerment or actual communication flows.
limitations: Public cable catalogs can omit or lag status, ownership and capacity changes.
Cataloged capacity is not lit, available or affordable capacity.
Centrality measures are sensitive to graph construction and aggregation level.
The analysis does not observe traffic, price, outages or terrestrial backhaul.
Digital-divide interpretation requires adoption, skills, affordability and governance evidence beyond cable topology.
anti_patterns: Do not equate centrality with throughput or service quality.
Do not infer campus access from a national landing.
Do not treat catalog capacity as usable capacity.
Do not use cable topology alone as a complete digital-divide measure.

candidate_population.title: Volcanic eruptions and the global subsea telecommunications network
candidate_population.candidate_study_type: global hazard review and case synthesis

verified_extraction.study_type: global historical case review of volcanic damage to subsea telecommunications cables
verified_extraction.claim_path: The review compiles cable damage associated with volcanic eruptions, traces multi-stage hazard cascades, identifies high-risk volcanic settings and evaluates route diversity, backup communications and cable-based sensing as mitigation.
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Cases combine industry records, historical accounts and geophysical studies. The <1% share refers to recorded global cable-damage instances, not the outage probability of a route near a volcano.
verified_extraction.quantitative_behavior: Volcanic damage is rare but can disconnect whole countries and produce effects lasting months to decades. No clear Volcanic Explosivity Index threshold separates damaging events; cascades involving mass movements and density currents dominate.
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Steep coastal/island volcanoes and shallow explosive systems are particularly concerning, but avoidance may be impossible for island access. Sparse routes and landing points amplify service consequences.
verified_extraction.causal_calibration: Case convergence supports hazard mechanisms and planning precautions but the rare-event sample cannot yield a portable causal failure rate.
limitations: Historical and industry reporting is incomplete.
Submarine volcano monitoring is sparse.
Events and cable configurations are highly heterogeneous.
VEI alone does not capture submarine mass movement and route exposure.
Backup feasibility depends on demand and finance in small island states.
anti_patterns: Do not infer zero risk from rarity.
Do not use VEI alone as a cable-risk score.
Do not call two cables resilient if they share volcanic corridors or landings.
Do not substitute satellite backup for equivalent capacity without qualification.

candidate_population.title: Submarine Cable Network Design for Regional Connectivity

verified_extraction.study_type: weighted-Steiner network optimization with proofs and realistic numerical scenarios
verified_extraction.claim_path: The paper formulates trunk-and-branch regional cable design as a weighted Steiner-node problem that includes cable laying, branching-unit and candidate landing-station costs, then demonstrates how cost assumptions change topology and station choice.
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Outputs minimize the encoded modeled cost on a triangulated manifold. Scenario dollar values, locations and terrain weights are design inputs, not vendor bids, permits or observed construction outcomes.
verified_extraction.quantitative_behavior: In one regional example, allowing alternative station costs selects a network 8% longer than the equal-cost solution while reducing the modeled total objective; a four-branch unit can slightly lower total cost despite greater cable length than a three-branch restriction.
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: The optimum changes with branching-unit cost, landing alternatives, seabed terrain, protected areas and topology constraints. A tree optimizes construction cost but does not itself deliver route redundancy.
verified_extraction.causal_calibration: Mathematical optimality holds for the specified model and discretization, not for unmodeled permitting, survey, market, repair or service-performance constraints.
limitations: Scenario costs are simplified and partly illustrative.
The topology is trunk-and-branch rather than a resilience mesh.
Environmental, legal and engineering details require richer input layers.
Numerical realism is not deployment validation.
The modeled objective omits traffic and outage consequences.
anti_patterns: Do not label an objective-optimal tree resilient.
Do not treat illustrative costs as bids.
Do not optimize station location without feasibility and backhaul.
Do not infer campus service from regional cable topology.

candidate_population.title: Who gets access to fast broadband? Evidence from Los Angeles County

verified_extraction.study_type: 2014-2018 Los Angeles County block-group panel with pooled and fixed-effects logistic models
verified_extraction.claim_path: The study combines CPUC provider-reported deployment data and ACS demographics, using broadband competition and residential fiber availability as proxies for investment, to test whether rollout differs by income and racial composition.
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: The full panel has 32,135 observations for 6,427 block groups over five years; reported model denominators vary because fixed-effects logit retains changing groups. Provider-reported availability means potential service to at least part of a block, not subscription or tested performance.
verified_extraction.quantitative_behavior: Predicted fiber availability is roughly three times lower in majority-Black than otherwise comparable block groups and approaches one-half in affluent areas versus about one-fifth in less-affluent areas. Associations persist in several fixed-effects specifications.
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Patterns are specific to LA County, 2014-2018, residential fixed broadband and the reporting regime. Race, income, housing value, gentrification, business demand and spatial aggregation can interact.
verified_extraction.causal_calibration: The authors characterize correlations, not a causal discriminatory-investment effect; time-varying omitted variables remain possible.
limitations: Provider reports can overstate service by marking a whole block served when one household is serviceable.
Advertised availability is not price, adoption or actual speed.
Competition and fiber are proxies for investment.
Time-varying omitted demand factors can bias estimates.
Block-group aggregation creates modifiable-areal-unit sensitivity.
anti_patterns: Do not equate availability with adoption or affordability.
Do not treat advertised coverage as measured performance.
Do not transport LA coefficients nationally without testing.
Do not infer causality from the demographic correlations.

candidate_population.title: Towards an internet-scale overlay network for latency-aware decentralized workflows at the edge
candidate_population.candidate_study_type: system design, prototype and active-measurement evaluation

verified_extraction.study_type: Viseu overlay architecture, RIPE Atlas path measurements and 27-node prototype benchmark
verified_extraction.claim_path: The paper motivates a latency-aware edge-service overlay, separates first-, middle- and last-mile path components, prototypes service selection across a research cluster and 21 AWS regions, and benchmarks selected endpoints against one Frankfurt cloud baseline.
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: Preliminary path examples use RIPE Atlas traceroute and ping. The prototype emulates 500 consumers with 500 Atlas probes; RTT uses 16 packets of 2,048 bytes. The deployment contains 27 workers, not a production Internet-scale service market.
verified_extraction.quantitative_behavior: Against the selected Frankfurt baseline, packet loss in one measurement attempt falls from 5.8% to 0.2%, and selected service instances generally reduce RTT and hops. Geographic proximity and hop count do not monotonically determine latency, and paths vary over time.
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Benefits depend on probe placement, time, cloud-region coverage, service replication, consumer location, routing and the single baseline. Last-mile bottlenecks can dominate even after a fast intercontinental middle mile.
verified_extraction.causal_calibration: The prototype comparison shows conditional engineering performance, not a general causal estimate for every edge overlay or proof of production reliability, security, economic adoption or scale.
limitations: The assessment is explicitly preliminary.
One Frankfurt server is the main baseline.
RIPE Atlas probe placement is biased.
The prototype is permissioned and includes only 27 workers.
Security, incentives and cross-organization deployment remain future work.
anti_patterns: Do not label prototype latency reductions universal.
Do not infer production adoption or SLA compliance.
Do not assume nearest geography yields the lowest latency.
Do not treat packet-loss tests as site capacity measurements.

candidate_population.title: O Peer, Where Art Thou? Uncovering Remote Peering Interconnections at IXPs
candidate_population.candidate_study_type: multi-dataset inference, validation and ecosystem characterization

verified_extraction.study_type: remote-peering inference using PeeringDB, IXP, RIPE Atlas, traceroute, port and validation data
verified_extraction.claim_path: The paper defines remote peering, demonstrates why latency-only inference fails, combines colocation, facility, RTT, port and connectivity signals, validates classifications and applies the method to 30 large IXPs.
verified_extraction.measurement_and_denominator: The ecosystem analysis covers 30 selected large IXPs; validation uses best-effort operator and public labels. The study processes 3.15 billion traceroutes from January 2017 to March 2018, but remote/local classifications still depend on observability and heuristic thresholds.
verified_extraction.quantitative_behavior: The method reports above 95% accuracy and 93% coverage per IXP versus 77% and 84% for the prior latency-only approach. About 28% of peers are inferred remote overall, reaching 40% at the largest IXPs; remote membership growth is roughly twice local growth.
verified_extraction.heterogeneity_and_regime: Wide-area IXPs, resellers, long cables, federations, shared ports and inflated RTTs complicate inference. A peer can be an IXP member without a router physically colocated at its switching fabric.
verified_extraction.causal_calibration: The study characterizes membership realization and dependency but does not measure all exchanged traffic or causally estimate remote peering’s performance and resilience effects.
limitations: Validation labels are best-effort and incomplete.
Port capacity and facility data can be stale or missing.
Traceroute and RTT can be asymmetric or inflated.
The 30-IXP sample emphasizes large exchanges.
Traffic-volume and longitudinal performance analysis are outside scope.
anti_patterns: Do not equate IXP membership with local physical presence.
Do not infer remote peering from RTT alone.
Do not count several remote peers on one reseller port as independent resilience.
Do not treat membership shares as traffic shares.

candidate_population.title: Metis: Selecting Diverse Atlas Vantage Points

verified_extraction.study_type: data-driven RIPE Atlas vantage-selection method with IPv4/IPv6 experiments and deployment recommendations

rhetoric.claim_path: Embeds a physical-to-IP cross-layer map, applies modular deterministic or probabilistic failure models, and produces risk profiles at cable-segment, AS, country, regional and global levels, then checks selected outputs against three real cable failures.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: The demonstration uses Nautilus definitely-submarine links and the top cable prediction, nearly one million observed IP links, cable-segment endpoints, IP geolocation and IP-to-AS mappings. Risk is the fraction of mapped links or entities exposed, not traffic volume or outage probability.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: Physical and IP-layer exposure can diverge sharply because link use is concentrated. Real-event comparisons sometimes align with reported traffic loss but diverge where cross-layer coverage, parallel cables, bandwidth and rerouting are missing.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: Results vary by disaster model, threshold, probability distribution, geography, landing dependence and network concentration; landlocked states may be exposed through neighboring landing systems.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: Xaminer is a scenario-analysis tool. It identifies modeled exposure and correlations, not causal effects, realized failure likelihood or post-failure service levels.
limitations: Nautilus mappings are incomplete and may select the wrong parallel cable.
Traceroute vantage points are biased toward Europe and North America.
Most analyses use cable endpoints and omit precise intermediate paths.
Risk-profile link fractions are not traffic-loss fractions.
BGP policy, load balancing, failover and bandwidth are unavailable.
anti_patterns: Do not equate exposed IP-link fraction with traffic loss.
Do not count parallel mapped cables as independent resilience.
Do not infer low risk from sparse measurement coverage.
Do not treat scenario output as failure probability.

citation.title: Impact of the first months of war on routing and latency in Ukraine

verified_admissions.study_type: longitudinal BGP, RIPE Atlas and topology measurement study

whole_text_evidence.access_note: Complete 11 numbered article pages through references; source PDF uses oversized multi-column sheets.

rhetoric.claim_path: Uses a ten-day pre-invasion baseline and about twelve weeks of RIPE RIS, RIPEstat and RIPE Atlas data to track routed ASes and prefixes, BGP updates, latency, path composition and Ukraine-Russia direct connectivity during the early war.
rhetoric.measurement_and_denominator: The study observes routes visible to RIPE collectors and active measurements from surviving Atlas probes and anchors between 14 February and 7 May 2022. It does not observe all networks, users, physical damage or traffic volumes.
rhetoric.quantitative_behavior: BGP announcements and withdrawals became more volatile, latency rose and became more variable, direct Ukraine-Russia AS links fell sharply, and paths increasingly involved Tier-1 transit. About 83% of initially connected Ukrainian probes remained connected in the last week.
rhetoric.heterogeneity_and_regime: Effects differ by direction, protocol, path pair, city and war phase; probe attrition and population movement alter the observed measurement base.
rhetoric.causal_calibration: Temporal overlap and path inspection support an association with the conflict and a partial peering-to-transit shift, but the study cannot separate physical destruction, operator policy, user movement and cyberattack causes.
limitations: The pre-war baseline is only ten days.
RIPE measurement infrastructure is not population representative.
Disconnected probes can disappear from latency denominators.
BGP anomalies are not uniquely attributable to attacks or physical damage.
The twelve-week window captures only the first war phase.
anti_patterns: Do not infer national service continuity from surviving probes alone.
Do not attribute every BGP update to cyberattack.
Do not treat nominal IXP availability as unchanged route use.
Do not generalize one conflict phase to persistent topology.

verified_atomic_observations.observation: IXP existence and membership do not complete the interconnection realization chain: operator willingness, peering policy, transport, cost and bilateral economics determine whether a route exchange and carried traffic materialize.
Geographically intra-regional endpoints can use intercontinental AS paths; route locality is an outcome of topology and peering structure, not endpoint proximity alone.

Reported path and RTT improvements are conditional counterfactual simulation results whose magnitude depends on topology, peering assumptions, geolocation, RTT inference and the absence of traffic-volume weighting.

A graph-theoretically short or inexpensive interconnection plan can be physically or institutionally infeasible when fiber availability, borders, security, investment and operator incentives are applied.
Public IXP/member datasets required operator validation and still contained unvalidated or estimated membership counts, establishing a measurable visibility boundary around public registries.
A minimum-link spanning-tree solution provides connectivity without redundancy; independent resilience requires additional links, backup hubs and shared-risk analysis.
Endpoint proximity does not determine path locality; interdomain topology and routing can send geographically local pairs through other countries or regions.
Route-locality estimates depend on vantage placement, IP geolocation coverage and whether countries are weighted by address space or population.
A measured traceroute path is one observed logical forwarding path and is not a measurement of all available physical routes or traffic volume.
Country-level locality percentages cannot establish bandwidth, redundancy, commercial access or service quality at a site.
Public CAIDA relationship labels and PeeringDB facility records are useful peering proxies but incomplete operational ground truth.
Co-location and geographic compatibility do not complete a peering decision; traffic, pricing, policy, stability and bilateral strategy remain material.
Peering-model performance changes with class balance and dataset construction, so a headline accuracy is conditional rather than portable.
A predicted peering pair or location is upstream of agreement, provisioning, route exchange, traffic and realized performance.
Logical IP links map probabilistically to one or more candidate physical submarine cables rather than to a directly observed single cable.
Multiple cable candidates for one IP link do not establish independent redundancy because landing points, owners, conduits and hazards may be shared.
MPLS, hidden hops, geolocation error and incomplete ownership data place an explicit visibility boundary on cross-layer cable maps.
Validation against selected failures and operator maps raises confidence in associations but does not make all inferred links physical ground truth.
The optimized undersea route depends on grid resolution, movement rules and cost-surface weights.
A lower modeled weighted cost is not a deployment-ready cable route; survey, bending, permitting, burial and commercial constraints remain.
Route optimization trades modeled risk/cost against computation time and can change ranking with the chosen objective.
Two separately computed candidate paths are not independent resilient routes unless shared landing, hazard and repair dependencies are tested.
Climate-driven cable hazard changes are spatially and temporally heterogeneous; a single global uplift factor cannot represent route-level risk.
Instantaneous extremes and sustained low-level currents or abrasion create different failure regimes over a cable design life.
A hazard hotspot marks exposure under scenarios, not an observed cable-specific outage probability.
Strategic chokepoints can force routes through shared hazards even when theoretical alternatives exist.
Natural hazards form a minority of recorded faults but can produce correlated damage across multiple cables and long segments.
Industry fault databases omit minor events and use overlapping inferred cause categories, bounding visibility and attribution.
A total route count masks regional differences in landing concentration, exposure and simultaneous-failure potential.
Complex, compound and cascading natural processes can delay or multiply connectivity failures beyond the initiating event.
Volcanic cable damage is rare in the global record but can disconnect single-cable countries for prolonged periods.
Volcanic Explosivity Index alone does not predict cable damage because route exposure and cascading mass movements mediate impact.
Geographic route and landing diversity, not nominal cable multiplicity, is the relevant resilience test near volcanoes.
Satellite backup may preserve minimal communications without replacing the capacity or performance of the severed subsea system.
A modeled minimum-cost cable tree can be longer geographically when landing-station and branching-unit costs are included.
Tree-topology construction efficiency is distinct from independent route redundancy.
Regional landing availability does not establish buildable station sites, terrestrial backhaul or campus access.
Optimization results are conditional on cost layers, candidate sites, terrain discretization and omitted constraints.
Provider-reported broadband availability can mark a whole area served when only part is serviceable.
Availability and advertised capability are not adoption, affordability, actual speed or institutional use.
Observed fiber and competition gaps vary with neighborhood income and racial concentration rather than following a simple citywide total.
Block-group panel associations do not identify a causal deployment effect and may retain time-varying omitted demand.
Public interconnection listings are a lower-bound view because private backbones, caches and bilateral links can be absent.
Listed port speed is neither observed traffic nor usable capacity at a customer or campus.
A public point may expose only some company services and says little about indirect customer dependency.
Interconnection presence is strongly geographically concentrated and company-specific rather than implied by national Internet totals.
Cable counts, listed capacity and graph centrality are different constructs from lit capacity, traffic and local service.
Country-level and landing-point centrality can yield different rankings because aggregation changes the dependency boundary.
A small core of landing points and corridors creates globally or regionally concentrated dependencies.
Physical cable expansion alone cannot establish adoption, affordability, skills or digital inclusion.
Last-mile latency or loss can dominate after a fast long-haul path, so end-to-end performance cannot be inferred from backbone proximity alone.
Geographic proximity and hop count are imperfect predictors of RTT and can vary over time.
Prototype overlay gains depend on selected vantage points, replicated locations and the baseline server.
Edge-resource presence is upstream of trust, discovery, provisioning, service execution and realized user performance.
IXP membership does not establish physical colocation: remote peers can connect by reseller, long cable or federation.
Several logical peer relationships may share one reseller port and fail together.
The networks indirectly dependent on remote peering extend beyond the visible IXP member list.
Latency alone cannot reliably classify remote peering; facility, port and topology evidence must be combined.
RIPE Atlas probe deployments are geographically and topologically concentrated, so default random selections inherit platform bias.
Vantage selection changes observed RTT, path, anycast and geographic distributions.
No single diversity metric is universal: RTT, AS-path and hop-based selection emphasize different regions and network properties.
Measurement visibility is outcome-specific and cannot be converted directly into local capacity or service availability.
Remote membership can grow while announced prefixes fall, so membership is not a proxy for carried reach.
Preference for remote over local announcements can create trombone paths despite nominal IXP connectivity.
Route-server observations omit bilateral sessions and prefix counts omit traffic volume.
Remote interfaces may be stable individually while retaining shared reseller or transport dependencies.
Degree sequence alone does not identify critical hubs, delivered performance or failure response.
Robustness must specify failure mode, layer, objective and resource constraints.
Engineered performance and protocol feedback cannot be recovered from topology-only models.
Random component loss and malicious fail-on behavior are different resilience regimes.
Installed cable length does not imply an equal disturbed footprint because burial concentrates near shallow approaches.
Modeled sediment disturbance is not equivalent to emitted carbon or realized climate impact.
Global route and sediment layers require uncertainty bounds rather than point claims.
Environmental externality varies with route depth, burial practice and local sediment rather than cable count alone.
Strategic-node rankings change with micro, meso and macro aggregation.
Capacity-weighted graph centrality is not lit traffic, local availability or outage consequence.
Major corridors concentrate geographic shared risk despite many cataloged cable systems.
Analyst-defined ports and channels condition structural results.
Physical coverage is upstream of affordability, devices, skills, competition and meaningful use.
National connectivity indicators conceal urban-rural and institutional heterogeneity.
Market structure and policy can block realization despite nominal network assets.
Secondary national indicators do not establish household or campus service quality.
Cable count and catalog design capacity do not establish sufficient, lit or independently routed national redundancy.
Territorial vulnerability changes across single, multiple and capacity-threshold failure scenarios.
Structural redundancy class is not an outage probability or consequence estimate.
Commercial incentives and development status shape where redundancy is built, so topology optimization is institutionally constrained.
Several cables sharing one canyon can fail in the same long-runout sediment event.
Cable hazard is episodic and conditional on river floods, sediment storage, tides and channel dynamics rather than route length alone.
Best-estimate and conservative-minimum erosion volumes differ because survey coverage and measurement uncertainty are material.
Observed physical hazard on a seabed route cannot be converted directly into network outage without routing and redundancy data.
A formal infrastructure-sharing mandate does not establish operational cooperation, use or service expansion.
Passive and active sharing have different technical, proprietary, maintenance and quality-of-service constraints.
Lower deployment cost can remain insufficient where rural demand, revenue and institutional capacity are weak.
Supply-side infrastructure availability does not resolve affordability, skills, content or gender barriers to adoption.
Physical cable exposure and IP-layer exposure can diverge sharply because logical use is concentrated on a subset of segments.
A landlocked state can depend heavily on submarine systems through neighboring countries despite having no domestic landing.
Mapped-link exposure is not traffic loss because bandwidth, routing policy, load balancing and failover are unobserved.
Hazard rankings change with event model, threshold, probability distribution, geographic granularity and cross-layer map quality.
Nominally connected countries can shift from direct peering and IXPs toward Tier-1 transit during disruption, increasing path length and latency.
BGP update surges are consistent with disruption but do not uniquely identify physical damage or cyberattack.
Surviving measurement probes provide a conditional resilience denominator and cannot represent users or disconnected probes.
Direct cross-border AS links can collapse while a large share of observed probes remains reachable through topology reconfiguration.

cross_text_production_rules: Name the layer: visible asset, physical route, logical path, commercial interconnection, carried traffic or realized performance.
State the denominator before the result and preserve unresolved cases instead of forcing classification.

Separate frequent local faults from correlated multi-route failures.
Use global studies for screening and local route/campus evidence for decisions.

universal_families.label: Visible infrastructure versus effective interconnection
universal_families.proposition: Public registries and membership lists may understate private, bilateral, remote or indirect interconnection, so observed infrastructure is a lower-bound view of effective connectivity.
universal_families.production_rule: Apply visible infrastructure versus effective interconnection as a mandatory qualification before translating public connectivity evidence into market or campus claims.

universal_families.label: Physical route versus logical path
universal_families.proposition: IP paths cannot be mapped to physical terrestrial or submarine routes without cross-layer inference and explicit uncertainty.
universal_families.production_rule: Apply physical route versus logical path as a mandatory qualification before translating public connectivity evidence into market or campus claims.

universal_families.label: National route totals versus local usable capacity
universal_families.proposition: A national cable, route or facility count does not establish bandwidth, port availability, latency, redundancy or commercial access at a specific campus.
universal_families.production_rule: Apply national route totals versus local usable capacity as a mandatory qualification before translating public connectivity evidence into market or campus claims.

universal_families.label: Geographic proximity versus path locality
universal_families.proposition: Geographically local endpoints may traverse distant networks because topology, peering policy and economics mediate route choice.
universal_families.production_rule: Apply geographic proximity versus path locality as a mandatory qualification before translating public connectivity evidence into market or campus claims.

universal_families.label: Route count versus independent resilience
universal_families.proposition: Multiple apparent routes can share landing stations, conduits, hazards, providers or repair dependencies and therefore need not provide independent redundancy.
universal_families.production_rule: Apply route count versus independent resilience as a mandatory qualification before translating public connectivity evidence into market or campus claims.

universal_families.label: Interconnection realization ladder
universal_families.proposition: Facility or IXP presence must be separated from physical access, provisioning, peering agreement, route exchange, carried traffic and realized performance.
universal_families.production_rule: Apply interconnection realization ladder as a mandatory qualification before translating public connectivity evidence into market or campus claims.

universal_families.label: Conditional capacity and performance
universal_families.proposition: Connectivity performance is conditional on topology, routing policy, congestion, time, measurement point and failure regime.
universal_families.production_rule: Apply conditional capacity and performance as a mandatory qualification before translating public connectivity evidence into market or campus claims.

universal_families.label: Availability versus adoption and use
universal_families.proposition: Public or municipal infrastructure availability does not guarantee institutional adoption, affordable service or realized traffic.
universal_families.production_rule: Apply availability versus adoption and use as a mandatory qualification before translating public connectivity evidence into market or campus claims.

universal_families.label: Membership versus dependency footprint
universal_families.proposition: Reported IXP membership is not equivalent to the set of networks, customers or traffic flows that depend directly or indirectly on the exchange.
universal_families.production_rule: Apply membership versus dependency footprint as a mandatory qualification before translating public connectivity evidence into market or campus claims.

universal_families.label: Optimization objective versus deployment feasibility
universal_families.proposition: A route, peering or topology optimum under a modeled objective does not establish buildability, commercial realization, regulatory approval or operational performance.
universal_families.production_rule: Apply optimization objective versus deployment feasibility as a mandatory qualification before translating public connectivity evidence into market or campus claims.

universal_claim_template: Object and layer: state whether the datum describes a system, landing, route, facility, port, member, session, path, capacity or traffic.

Denominator: state what was counted and what public/private activity is unobserved.
Geography: distinguish national, state, metro, facility and campus resolution.
Qualification: state inference uncertainty, shared-risk dependencies and commercial realization limits.
Permitted conclusion: make only the narrow claim supported at that layer.

known_boundaries: The corpus establishes defensible claim logic, measurement limits and rhetoric; it is not a live market database.
Public registries are lower-bound visibility into private and bilateral connectivity.
System, route, facility and membership counts do not establish traffic, spare capacity, commercial access or campus service.
Cross-layer maps, geolocation and traceroutes remain inference- and sampling-limited.
Resilience requires physical, provider, landing, conduit, hazard and repair independence, not merely multiple labels.
Global and national evidence supports screening; facility and campus decisions require local technical and commercial verification.

basis: All 30 discovered candidates have terminal states: 25 admitted, 2 audit-blocked, 3 screened out with no claims retained.
All 25 admissions have unique DOIs, current JIF >=2, complete-text access and complete substantive-section review.
Ten universal families are supported by 102 verified atomic observations across multiple sources.
Two independent five-source post-foundation challenges each added zero universal families and reopened no material gap.
Fourteen long-form passage analyses were completed across two complete texts.
Production mappings preserve source layer, denominator, geography, uncertainty, shared-risk and campus boundaries.
